image.caption: Rāma stalks Mārīca in the form of a golden deer, Mughal painting from Akbar's Rāmāyaṇa

versions.title: The Fox Who Became a Woman
versions.teaser: At fifty a fox can become a woman; at a thousand it reaches Heaven.
versions.text:
Chinese lore gives the fox a career. 'When a fox is fifty years old,' says a fourth-century text attributed to Guo Pu, 'it can change into a woman. At a hundred it becomes a beautiful girl, or a shaman, or a man who sleeps with women. It can know things a thousand li away, and it can bewitch people until they lose their wits. At a thousand years it communicates with Heaven and becomes a heavenly fox.'

Gan Bao's collection of strange tales from the same period includes the soldier Wang Lingxiao, who deserts and cannot be found. He is at last discovered in an empty grave, having taken on the look of a fox. He says that a beautiful woman named A Zi kept calling to him. 'The fox,' says an old book Gan Bao quotes, 'was a lewd woman of ancient times, and her name was A Zi.'

These foxes are still frightening. The affectionate, clever fox-women of Pu Songling's Liaozhai came more than a thousand years later.

versions.title: The Fox Wife of Mino
versions.teaser: A man's wife is revealed as a fox; he asks her back.
versions.text:
In the reign of Emperor Kinmei, a man of Mino province rides out looking for a good wife. In a wide field he meets a lovely woman who is willing to marry him. They wed, and she bears him a son. But their dog, which gave birth at the same time, hates her, and its puppy barks at her whenever she passes.

One day the dog goes for her. She is terrified, turns back into a fox, and jumps up onto the fence. Her husband calls after her: 'You and I have a child together, and I cannot forget you. Come and sleep with me always.' So she keeps coming back to sleep with him. Because of this she is called kitsu-ne, 'come and sleep', and that is why the fox is called kitsune.

Their son, named Kitsune-no-atai, grows immensely strong and swift, and his line are known in Mino as the foxes' descendants.
versions.caveat: The 'come and sleep' etymology is a folk etymology the text itself offers.

versions.title: Vseslav the Wolf-Prince
versions.teaser: By day he judged men; by night he ran as a wolf.
versions.text:
Prince Vseslav of Polotsk was a historical ruler of the eleventh century, and he was famous for his sorcery. The Primary Chronicle says his mother bore him through enchantment, with a caul over his head, and that the magicians told her to bind it on him to wear for life.

The Tale of Igor's Campaign turns him into a werewolf. 'Prince Vseslav judged the people, he ruled cities for princes, but in the night he prowled as a wolf. From Kiev he raced before the cocks crowed to Tmutarakan, and as a wolf he crossed the path of great Khors.' When the bells rang for matins at St Sophia in Polotsk, he heard them in Kiev.

The folk hero of the byliny, Volkh Vseslavyevich, has the same name and gift. He turns into a falcon, a grey wolf, a golden-horned aurochs and even an ant to lead his army.
sources: Tale of Igor's Campaign (Slovo o polku Igoreve)
versions.caveat: The authenticity of the Tale of Igor's Campaign, known only from a manuscript lost in 1812, has been disputed, though most scholars accept it as medieval.

versions.title: Sigmund and Sinfjötli in Wolfskins
versions.teaser: Father and son put on enchanted wolfskins and cannot take them off.
versions.text:
Sigmund, the Völsung, is training his son Sinfjötli in the forest to take revenge. One day they find a house where two men lie asleep wearing thick gold rings, with wolfskins hanging above them. The men are under a spell and can leave the skins only every tenth day.

Sigmund and Sinfjötli put the skins on and cannot take them off. They howl like wolves and understand each other's howling. They split up, agreeing that each will howl for help if he meets more than seven men. Sinfjötli meets eleven and kills them all without calling. In a rage, Sigmund bites him in the throat, then carries him home grieving. He sees a weasel bite another and heal it with a leaf, and a raven brings Sigmund the same leaf, which cures his son.

When the tenth day comes, they take off the skins and burn them, so that they can do no further harm.
versions.caveat: The saga dates from the 13th century; the episode is often linked to wolf-warrior (úlfheðnar) traditions, but that link is inferred.

versions.title: Gwion Bach and Ceridwen
versions.teaser: A chase through every shape ends with a hen swallowing a grain of wheat.
versions.text:
Ceridwen, a sorceress living by Llyn Tegid, has a son so ugly that she decides to give him the gift of knowledge. She boils a cauldron of herbs for a year and a day, and sets the boy Gwion Bach to stir it. Near the end, three scalding drops land on his finger, and he sucks it. At once he knows everything, including that Ceridwen will kill him. The cauldron cracks and the rest of the brew turns to poison.

He runs as a hare, and she follows as a greyhound. He jumps into a river as a fish, and she pursues as an otter. He becomes a bird, and she a hawk. At last he drops into a heap of winnowed wheat as a single grain. She becomes a black hen and swallows him.

Nine months later she gives birth to him. Unable to kill so beautiful a baby, she sets him adrift in a leather bag. He is found at a fish-weir and named Taliesin, 'radiant brow'.
versions.caveat: The prose tale is first recorded in the 16th century, though the poems ascribed to Taliesin that allude to his many shapes are earlier.

image.caption: Ceridwen's cauldron, print by J. E. C. Williams in Y Mabinogion (Wrexham, 1901)

versions.title: Māui as a Pigeon
versions.teaser: The trickster puts on a pigeon's form to follow his mother below the earth.
versions.text:
Every night Māui's mother Taranga sleeps with her children, and every dawn she vanishes. Māui, the youngest, wants to know where she goes. He blocks the gaps in the house so no daylight gets in. Then, when she slips away at sunrise, he watches her pull up a clump of rushes and disappear down a hole into the earth.

Māui takes the form of a kererū, the wood pigeon. In Grey's account, his mother's belt becomes the white feathers on the bird's breast. He flies down the hole into the underworld and perches in a tree above a group of people sitting on the grass. He drops berries on them until his mother and father look up and recognize him. His father takes him to the water for a naming rite, but the words are said wrongly. The mistake will cost Māui his life when he later tries to win immortality.
versions.caveat: Grey's text is an edited compilation from Māori manuscripts, and details such as the pigeon's colouring vary between tellings.
